A flowchart is a diagram that shows a process, system, or workflow as a series of steps connected by arrows. It turns something that happens over time — a sequence of actions and decisions — into something you can see all at once on a single page.

Think of it like a map, but instead of showing you where to go geographically, it shows you what to do next in a process.
What It Looks Like

A flowchart is made of shapes connected by arrows. Each shape has a specific meaning, and the arrows tell you the direction of flow — where the process goes next.

The most common shapes are:

  • Oval / Rounded rectangle — Marks the Start or End of the process. Every flowchart begins and ends here.
  • Rectangle — Represents an action or a step — something that is done. For example: "Send the email" or "Bake the cake."
  • Diamond — Represents a decision point — a yes/no or true/false question. The process branches into two or more paths depending on the answer. For example: "Is the password correct?" → one arrow goes to Yes, another to No.
  • Parallelogram — Represents input (something entering the process, like a user typing data) or output (something being produced, like a printed receipt).
  • Arrow — Connects all shapes and shows the direction in which the process moves.
How It Works

You read a flowchart by following the arrows, starting from the Start oval. You move through steps (rectangles) one by one. When you reach a diamond, you answer the question inside it, and then follow the arrow that matches your answer. Eventually, every path leads to the End oval.

The key insight is that a flowchart models logic — the "if this, then that" kind of thinking. It makes the logic of a process visible, so anyone reading it can follow the exact same path a person or system would follow in real life.
A Simple Example

Imagine the process of logging into a website:

  1. Start
  2. Enter username and password (action)
  3. Is the password correct? (decision)
    • Yes → Go to the homepage (action) → End
    • No → Show "Wrong password" message (action) → Go back to step 2

This entire logic — which could take a paragraph of words to describe — can be drawn as a small, clear flowchart that anyone can understand in seconds.
Why Flowcharts Exist

Before flowcharts, people described processes in plain text or verbal instructions. The problem with text is that it is linear — you read it one sentence at a time — and it is easy to get confused when a process branches into multiple possibilities.

A flowchart solves this by making the structure of a process visible. You can immediately see how many decision points exist, how many paths are possible, and where each path leads. This visual clarity is the whole point.
Where Flowcharts Are Used

Flowcharts appear in almost every field where a process needs to be understood, communicated, or improved:

  • Computer science and programming — Programmers draw flowcharts to plan the logic of a program before writing any code. It helps them think through all possible scenarios (including errors) before they begin.
  • Business and management — Companies use flowcharts to map out workflows — for example, how a customer complaint is handled, or how an order is processed from purchase to delivery.
  • Manufacturing — Factories use flowcharts to describe assembly processes and quality checks.
  • Medicine and healthcare — Doctors and hospitals use flowcharts (often called clinical pathways or decision trees) to guide diagnosis and treatment decisions.
  • Education — Teachers use flowcharts to explain processes in science, history, and other subjects.
  • Everyday life — Even a simple decision like "Should I carry an umbrella today?" can be drawn as a tiny flowchart: Is it cloudy? → Yes → Is rain forecast? → Yes → Carry an umbrella.
Types of Flowcharts

While the word "flowchart" most commonly refers to the standard type described above, there are variations with specific names and purposes:

  • Process flowchart — The most common kind. Maps the steps of any process from start to finish.
  • Swimlane flowchart (also called a cross-functional flowchart) — Divides the diagram into horizontal or vertical lanes, each lane representing a different person, team, or department. This makes it clear who is responsible for each step. For example, a swimlane flowchart for processing a job application might have separate lanes for the applicant, the HR team, and the hiring manager.
  • Data flow diagram (DFD) — Focuses specifically on how data moves through a system (where it comes from, where it goes, and where it is stored). Used heavily in software design.
  • Workflow diagram — Similar to a process flowchart but usually focuses on people and their responsibilities rather than technical steps.
  • Decision tree — A flowchart that consists almost entirely of decision diamonds, branching outward into more and more specific outcomes. Used in data analysis, medicine, and artificial intelligence.
Why People Use Flowcharts

Flowcharts are popular because they serve several powerful purposes:

  1. Clarity — They make complex processes easy to understand at a glance, even for someone who has never seen the process before.
  2. Communication — They give everyone involved in a process a shared, unambiguous picture of how it works. This reduces misunderstandings.
  3. Problem-solving — When a process is broken or inefficient, drawing a flowchart often reveals exactly where the problem lies — a missing step, a decision point with no clear path, or an unnecessary loop.
  4. Documentation — Flowcharts serve as a permanent record of how a process works, so that new employees or future teams can quickly learn it.
  5. Planning — Before building something complex (like software or a factory workflow), a flowchart lets you test the logic on paper before investing real time and resources.
Common Mistakes and Limitations

A flowchart, despite its usefulness, has limits worth knowing:

  • Oversimplification — Very complex processes can produce enormous, messy flowcharts that become hard to read. In such cases, the process is often broken into multiple smaller flowcharts that reference each other.
  • Static nature — A flowchart captures a process as it is at one point in time. If the process changes, the flowchart must be updated, or it becomes misleading.
  • No details inside shapes — Each shape in a flowchart is a label, not a full instruction. The rectangle "Send the email" doesn't tell you what to write in the email. Flowcharts show structure, not detail.
  • Not suitable for all processes — Highly parallel processes (where many things happen simultaneously) are difficult to represent clearly in a traditional flowchart. Other diagram types (like Gantt charts or network diagrams) are used instead.
The Essence of the Word

To put it in the simplest terms possible: a flowchart is a picture of a process. It uses shapes and arrows to show what happens, in what order, and what choices are made along the way. The word itself reflects this perfectly — flow (the movement through steps) + chart (a visual diagram). It is one of the most universal tools for thinking clearly and communicating a process to others.
